### Part 2 --- Evidence, models, and inference

The conceptual core. What a causal claim is, what the standard models estimate, where uncertainty comes from, the difference between explaining and predicting, and how inference goes wrong — taught on examples from industry and the news, before anyone opens a dataset. Teams form in the first meeting of this part, and it closes by writing the problem up and presenting it.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 2 | Sep 2 | **Causal language**<br><span class='goal'>Draw your own project's causal graph, say which variable you must condition on and which you must not touch, and leave with a signed team charter.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Counterfactuals and potential outcomes; why every comparison is a claim about a world that did not happen. Causal graphs: confounders, colliders, mediators, back-door reasoning — and why controlling for everything makes things worse<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Team formation and the team charter. The conflict protocol and the division of labour, agreed in writing now rather than negotiated in November: who does what, what happens when somebody misses a deadline, and when to escalate to me. The weekly stand-up starts today | Team charter, same day |
| 3 | Sep 9 | **Models, uncertainty, and prediction**<br><span class='goal'>Read a coefficient in the units of the problem, say what a p-value does and does not tell you, and tell an explanatory question apart from a predictive one.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Linear regression, non-linear models, and count models — described, not derived: what each estimates and how to read a coefficient in the units of the problem. Then where uncertainty comes from: residuals and errors, sampling variation, what a standard error states, where p-values come from and what they are not. Finally the distinction that decides half the projects in this room — explaining versus predicting, and why a model that predicts well may tell you nothing about what to do<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Simulation lab: draw from a world you control. Watch the p-value distribution under the null, then change the sample size and the variation and watch it move. The ways applied economists get a credible estimate, from conditioning on observables to designs built on found variation — what variation each exploits, what each assumes, and how each fails.

### Part 4 --- Measurement, data, and getting hold of it

The step most projects skip. Turning a construct into something a dataset can hold, working out what the design actually demands, and then the practical business of obtaining it — sources, proprietary access, data-use agreements, the IRB, and what scraping and APIs can and cannot get you.

| \# | Date | Meeting | Due |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 9 | Oct 21\* | **Measurement, and what the design demands**<br><span class='goal'>Turn your central construct into a variable somebody could actually record, and specify the unit, frequency, span, and coverage your design demands.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> Constructs and operationalization: how you turn 'sustainability', 'financial literacy', or 'market power' into a variable somebody could actually record, and what makes that measure defensible or indefensible. Validity, and what a proxy costs you. Then working backwards from the design to its data requirements: unit of observation, level of aggregation, time frequency, span, coverage, and which comparisons the data has to contain — can this be done with county-level data, or does it need individuals?<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> What to ask of a dataset before trusting anything it says: what is one row? how many are there? what is missing, and is it missing at random? what is the range, and are the extremes real? what changed over time, and did the definition change with it? Then the measurement clinic — the variable your question actually needs, and whether anything on earth measures it | Writing 2 — limitation paragraph |
| 10 | Oct 28 | **Getting hold of the data**<br><span class='goal'>Name your data source, its access route, its timeline, and your plan B — and know whether you need IRB approval or a data-use agreement before January.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> The landscape: administrative records, official statistics, firm and platform data, purchased panels — what each costs in money and in months. Proprietary access and data-use agreements: who signs, how long it takes, and what they forbid you from publishing. Research ethics and the Cornell IRB: what needs approval, what does not, and how long it takes. Then scraping and APIs at awareness level — what they are, what they can and cannot get you, what the terms of service and the law actually say, and when paying for a licence is the cheaper answer. We do not write scrapers in this course; you need to know what to ask for and what it costs<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Academic writing II — the memo. Writing to a decision-maker rather than an examiner: the two-page discipline, the bottom line first, and the fallback that shows you thought about failure. Then the acquisition clinic: each team names its source, its access route, its timeline, and its plan B | Data feasibility memo assigned |
| 11 | Nov 4 | **Midterm; interrogating data with an assistant**<br><span class='goal'>Design a study in writing under exam conditions; then interrogate a real dataset through an assistant and catch something that is wrong with it.</span><br><span class='sess'>A · 2:05</span> **Midterm** — you are given a situation and asked to design a study to evaluate it, in writing: the question, the design, what data it requires, and what would undermine it<br><span class='sess'>B · 3:35</span> Real data in front of you, and the checklist from meeting 9 put to work through an assistant: summaries, joins, quick plots.
